title: Aorto-Pulmonary Shunt Creation in Congenital Heart Disease: Different Indications, Various Modifications, but Common Technical Challenges
authors: Matija Bakoš; Stanimir G. Georgiev; Kerstin Wustman; Paul Philipp Heinisch; Kristina Borgmann; Dunja Renner; Andreas Eicken; Julia Lemmer; Peter Ewert; Katarzyna Karolina Gendera
abstract: Percutaneous creation of an aorto-pulmonary (AP) shunt has been explored in preclinical models for over 15 years, yet its clinical application remains limited. Surgical AP shunts are widely used to augment pulmonary blood flow in cyanotic congenital heart disease, but repeated thoracic operations and general anesthesia carry substantial risks in critically ill or surgically complex patients. A less invasive transcatheter alternative could therefore represent a transformative option. We report a case series of two pediatric patients in whom a percutaneous connection between the aorta and pulmonary artery was successfully established. Indications were severe cyanosis due to compromised pulmonary blood flow in one child and suprasystemic pulmonary arterial hypertension requiring decompression in the other. The procedures were technically feasible and resulted in the intended immediate hemodynamic effects, either by enhancing pulmonary perfusion or by enabling right-to-left shunting for right heart decompression. Conceptually, percutaneous AP shunt creation parallels the transcatheter Potts shunt, which is increasingly recognized as a therapeutic option in pulmonary arterial hypertension. Both approaches establish controlled communication between the aorta and pulmonary artery, adapted to distinct physiological settings. Our report represents, to our knowledge, the first description of percutaneous AP shunt creation to improve pulmonary blood flow and oxygenation in congenital heart disease, as well as the first percutaneous connection between the ascending aorta and the pulmonary artery. These cases illustrate the technical feasibility of catheter-based AP shunt creation in selected pediatric patients and support further evaluation of this approach.

title: Secondary Intervention Burden After Fenestrated Endovascular Aortic Repair: A Patient-Level and Procedure-Level Analysis of a 14-Year Single-Center Experience
authors: Alexandre Rossillon; Nicolas Massad; Robin Sagnet; Mauricio Gonzalez Urquijo; Pierre‐Edouard Magnan; Michel Alain Bartoli
abstract: Purpose: To quantify the patient-level and procedure-level burden, concentration, timing, and characteristics of secondary interventions after fenestrated endovascular aortic repair (FEVAR), and their association with subsequent mortality. Materials and Methods: This retrospective single-center study included 189 consecutive patients treated with FEVAR between 2007 and 2021. Secondary interventions were classified by clinical magnitude, approach, timing, and primary indication. The cumulative incidence of a first secondary intervention was estimated using the Aalen-Johansen method with death as a competing event. The association with subsequent mortality was assessed using a time-dependent Cox model. Results: Technical success was achieved in 185 of 189 patients (97.9%). Median observed follow-up was 40.9 months (interquartile range, 25.1-61.2), and median potential follow-up was 57.4 months. Forty-eight patients (25.4%) underwent 67 secondary procedures. Nine patients, representing 4.8% of the cohort, underwent repeated interventions and accounted for 28 procedures (41.8%). Of the 67 procedures, 25 (37.3%) were major, 42 (62.7%) were minor, and 52 (77.6%) were endovascular. Thirty-seven procedures (55.2%) occurred more than 1 year after FEVAR. The 48-month cumulative incidence of a first secondary intervention was 24.7%, compared with 27.0% using 1 minus Kaplan-Meier. At the last available imaging examination, 610 of 615 assessable fenestrated target vessels were patent (99.2%). Secondary intervention was not statistically associated with subsequent mortality (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.11; 95% confidence interval, 0.68-1.80; P = .687). Conclusion: Secondary interventions affected approximately one quarter of patients after FEVAR, but a small subgroup accounted for a disproportionate share of the procedural burden. Most procedures were minor and endovascular, and more than half occurred beyond 1 year. No statistically significant average association with subsequent mortality was identified. Reporting both patient- and procedure-level burden may better characterize FEVAR durability and follow-up requirements. Clinical Impact Secondary interventions after fenestrated endovascular aortic repair (FEVAR) are commonly reported as the proportion of patients undergoing at least 1 procedure, which does not capture cumulative procedural burden. In this cohort of 189 patients, 48 underwent 67 secondary interventions, whereas only 9 patients, representing 4.8% of the cohort, accounted for 41.8% of all procedures. Most interventions were minor and endovascular, but more than half occurred beyond 1 year. These findings indicate that first reintervention rates alone incompletely describe FEVAR durability. Reporting both patient- and procedure-level burden may better inform patient counseling, surveillance planning, and comparisons across devices and centers by highlighting the concentration of procedures in a small subgroup.

title: Segundo consenso de postura sobre los aneurismas de aorta abdominal en México
authors: Luis F. Flota-Cervera; Alfonso Cossío-Zazueta; Abdel Kerim Raffoul Orozco; Javier E. Anaya‐Ayala
abstract: resumen Antecedentes: El aneurisma de aorta abdominal (AAA) es una enfermedad progresiva y potencialmente letal cuya ruptura puede alcanzar una mortalidad de hasta el 80% en México.La limitada evidencia epidemiológica nacional y la necesidad de estandarizar criterios diagnósticos, terapéuticos y de seguimiento motivaron la elaboración del Segundo Consenso Nacional sobre AAA en México, coordinado por la Sociedad Mexicana de Angiología, Cirugía Vascular y Endovascular (SMACVE), con base en las guías de la Society for Vascular Surgery y su adaptación al contexto nacional.Método: El consenso se desarrolló mediante el método RAND/UCLA y un proceso Delphi modificado.Se evaluaron 116 enunciados derivados de las guías de la Society for Vascular Surgery por un panel de expertos nacionales e internacionales.Los enunciados fueron discutidos, reformulados cuando fue necesario y sometidos a votación estructurada.Se definió el consenso como un acuerdo de ≥ 80%.resultados: Se alcanzó consenso en la mayoría de los enunciados evaluados, incluidos recomendaciones sobre tamizaje, diagnóstico, valoración preoperatoria, manejo médico, indicaciones de reparación endovascular y abierta, tratamiento de la ruptura, cuidados perioperatorios, seguimiento y aspectos organizativos.Las recomendaciones fueron adaptadas a las condiciones de práctica clínica y disponibilidad de recursos del sistema de salud mexicano.conclusiones: Este consenso proporciona definiciones, criterios diagnósticos y recomendaciones terapéuticas estandarizadas para la atención del AAA en México, con el objetivo de favorecer una práctica clínica homogénea, basada en evidencia y adaptada a las condiciones locales.

title: Reproducibility dataset for: Experimental validation of spectral redistribution theory in intracranial aneurysm and aortic valve flow
authors: Khalid M. Saqr
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This research object contains the data products, analysis code, provenance records, quality control outputs, figure source data, and final figures supporting the study “Experimental validation of spectral redistribution theory in intracranial aneurysm and aortic valve flow.” The study extends the theoretical framework introduced by Khalid M. Saqr in “Resonant spectral cascade in Womersley flow triggered by arterial geometry,” Physics of Fluids 38, 041901, 2026, DOI 10.1063/5.0319995. That work predicted that geometric modulation of pulsatile arterial flow can redistribute wave energy across axial spatial scales. A central prediction of the theory is that increased relative energy at higher axial wavenumbers can occur while the total wave energy is decreasing. The present experimental analysis examines that prediction directly in measured spatial velocity fields. Two independent experimental datasets provide the basis of the study. The intracranial aneurysm analysis uses the experimental measurements reported by Brindise and colleagues in “Multi modality cerebral aneurysm haemodynamic analysis in vivo 4D flow MRI, in vitro volumetric particle velocimetry and in silico computational fluid dynamics,” Journal of the Royal Society Interface, DOI 10.1098/rsif.2019.0465. The corresponding public dataset is hosted by the Purdue University Research Repository under the record “In vitro Volumetric Particle Velocimetry, Computational Fluid Dynamics CFD, and in vivo 4D Flow MRI Hemodynamic Data in Two Patient Specific Cerebral Aneurysms.” The present work uses the volumetric particle tracking measurements from the ANY007 model. These measurements permit direct evaluation of axial spectral structure across the global field and within anatomically defined regions including the parent artery, aneurysm neck, core, and dome. The aortic valve analysis uses the measurements reported by Till Zeugin and colleagues in “In vitro investigation of the blood flow downstream of a 3D printed aortic valve,” Scientific Reports, DOI 10.1038/s41598-024-51676-6. The corresponding source dataset is hosted by ETH Zurich under DOI 10.3929/ethz-b-000559354. It contains three dimensional particle tracking velocimetry measurements for four flow configurations comprising a 3D printed aortic valve, two transcatheter aortic valve implantation configurations, and a severe stenosis condition. These four cases provide an independent experimental test of the spectral analysis across distinct valve geometries and flow states. For both datasets, the measured velocity field is projected onto a fixed streamwise path defined from the experimental geometry and phase averaged flow. The streamwise residual velocity is evaluated directly as a function of spatial position and cardiac phase. Its axial spatial spectrum is then calculated from the measured spatial coordinates. No temporal frequency to wavenumber conversion is used. The analysis quantifies the total wave energy, its instantaneous logarithmic growth or decay rate, and the ratio between high and low axial wavenumber energy. The resulting measurements show phase dependent redistribution of spectral energy toward higher axial wavenumbers. The response varies with anatomical region and valve condition. In the aneurysm model, the strongest redistribution is localized within the aneurysm dome and is substantially reduced by whole domain averaging. Across the aortic valve cases, spectral redistribution occurs over distinct portions of the pulsatile cycle and differs among the four configurations. The energetic analysis identifies intervals in which total wave energy decreases while the relative high wavenumber contribution increases. This observation provides the experimental benchmark for the central spectral prediction of the published theory and establishes that spectral redistribution and total wave energy growth are dynamically separable quantities in measured arterial flow fields. The experimental scope addresses the directly observable spatial spectral signature predicted by the theory. The present datasets do not provide a controlled Womersley number sweep, so the Womersley dependent resonant response identified in the theoretical study remains a subject for dedicated experiments. The deposited archive contains the complete analysis notebook, the final figure reconstruction notebook, derived numerical products, spectral diagnostics, bootstrap results, quality control records, processing provenance, figure source data, final publication figures, and software environment specifications. The original third party experimental datasets are not redistributed. Their published papers and hosted source records are identified through the related works associated with this Zenodo deposit so that the complete analysis can be reconstructed from the original measurements.

title: Very Early-Onset Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis Following Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation Complicated by an Aorto-Left Atrial Fistula and Aortic Root Pseudoaneurysm
authors: Giulio D'ascoli; Jesús Piqueras‐Flores; Carlos Sánchez Sánchez; Fernando Lozano Ruíz-Poveda
abstract: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is an established treatment for severe aortic stenosis.Infective endocarditis (IE) is an uncommon but potentially devastating complication, typically presenting weeks to months after valve implantation.Very early-onset prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE), occurring within 48 hours of implantation, poses a particular diagnostic challenge, as infectious complications must be distinguished from procedure-related structural injury and sterile postprocedural inflammatory changes.We report the case of an 81-year-old man who underwent transfemoral TAVI with a self-expanding Evolut FX valve for severe symptomatic aortic stenosis.The procedure was uneventful, with satisfactory immediate angiographic and echocardiographic findings.Within 48 hours, the patient developed fever and elevated inflammatory markers.Two independent blood culture sets were positive for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA).Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (FDG-PET/CT) demonstrated increased metabolic uptake at the aortic root.Given the early postprocedural timing, this finding was interpreted cautiously, as sterile inflammatory changes could not be excluded.Subsequent transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) revealed a prosthetic valve vegetation, an aortic-root pseudoaneurysm, and an aorto-left atrial fistula with continuous shunt flow.The combination of microbiological and echocardiographic findings fulfilled the diagnostic criteria for definite prosthetic valve IE.Surgical intervention was considered prohibitive by the multidisciplinary Heart Team, and antimicrobial treatment was administered.Despite treatment, the patient's clinical condition rapidly deteriorated, resulting in death within one week of diagnosis.This case highlights the importance of integrating clinical and microbiological findings with multimodality imaging in diagnosing very early-onset PVE, while carefully considering potential procedure-related structural injury.

title: Aortic valve replacement in a patient with neurofibromatosis type 1: surgical considerations and perioperative management
authors: Tanushree Kar; Ashwani Bansal; Ankit Singhal
abstract: Abstract Introduction Cardiovascular involvement has been described in patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), including congenital cardiac abnormalities, hypertension, and vascular lesions; however, clinically significant valvular disease requiring cardiac surgery is rarely reported. We report a case of severe aortic regurgitation (AR) in a patient with NF1 and highlight the perioperative evaluation, surgical decision-making, and management considerations relevant to cardiac surgery in this multisystem disorder. A 67-year-old female with NF1 presented with progressive dyspnea and was diagnosed with severe aortic regurgitation. Following comprehensive cardiovascular and perioperative evaluation, she successfully underwent bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement (AVR) with an uneventful recovery. Severe aortic regurgitation in patients with NF1 should be evaluated and managed according to established guidelines for valvular heart disease. Given the possibility of multisystem involvement, a thorough perioperative evaluation of patients with NF1 undergoing cardiac surgery remains paramount. A multidisciplinary and individually tailored approach is important, given the diverse systemic manifestations. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Association of CTA-derived carotid plaque imaging features with 1-year ischemic stroke risk: An exploratory analysis
authors: Ke Li; Jin Ban; Lin Yuan
journal: Journal of Radiation Research and Applied Sciences
abstract: Objective This investigation was designed to explore the relationship between the imaging characteristics of carotid plaques and the likelihood of experiencing ischemic stroke during 1-year follow-up, utilizing computed tomography angiography as the primary imaging modality. Methods Computed tomography angiography (CTA) was employed to acquire cervical arterial images. Plaques were classified by computed tomography (CT) attenuation into a single prespecified four-category scheme: lipid-rich (<60 Hounsfield units [HU]), fibrous (60–130 HU), calcified (>130 HU), and mixed (containing two or more components). Surface morphology was assessed separately as regular or irregular. These attenuation-defined categories are semi-quantitative imaging phenotypes and are not histopathologically validated. To evaluate the associations between plaque composition, morphological features, volumetric measurements, the extent of luminal narrowing, and the subsequent risk of stroke during 1-year follow-up, multivariate logistic regression modeling was applied. The primary endpoint for the primary analysis was recurrent ischemic stroke in the observation group; first-ever ischemic stroke in the control group was described separately. Results A total of 200 participants were analyzed, including 100 with baseline ischemic stroke in the observation group and 100 without baseline ischemic stroke in control group. During 1-year follow-up, 29 patients in the observation group had recurrent ischemic stroke, and 5 participants in the control group had first-ever ischemic stroke. The primary analysis was restricted to recurrent events in the observation group; recurrent and incident events were not pooled. Severe stenosis or complete occlusion of the carotid artery was observed predominantly in the observation group, whereas only two instances of mild narrowing were identified in the control group. A total of 118 carotid plaques were detected: 103 in the observation group and 15 in the control group. Using the single prespecified four-category scheme, the 118 plaques comprised 27 lipid-rich plaques (22.88%), 54 fibrous plaques (45.76%), 19 calcified plaques (16.10%), and 18 mixed plaques (15.25%). In the observation group, the 103 plaques were classified as lipid-rich (n = 26), fibrous (n = 46), calcified (n = 15), and mixed (n = 16). In the control group, the 15 plaques were classified as lipid-rich (n = 1), fibrous (n = 8), calcified (n = 4), and mixed (n = 2). The marked intergroup disparity was observed in the prevalence of carotid stenosis, which reached statistical significance ( P < 0.05). Adjusted associations were observed for irregular morphology (OR 3.648, 95% CI 1.049–12.69), plaque volume (OR 2.832, 95% CI 1.282–6.261), and lipid-rich plaque (OR 1.453, 95% CI 1.164–1.814). Irregular morphology, greater plaque volume, and lipid-rich composition were associated with recurrent ischemic stroke in the observation group during 1-year follow-up. Specifically, increases in both plaque volume and lipid content were associated with a heightened risk of recurrent ischemic stroke in the observation group. Conclusion CTA provides clear visualization of key carotid plaque features. Lipid-rich plaques, irregular surface contours, and larger plaque volumes were associated with an increased risk of recurrent ischemic stroke in the observation group during the 1-year follow-up. CTA-derived plaque morphology, volume, and lipid-rich composition may be considered candidate markers for 1-year ischemic stroke risk stratification, pending prospective external validation.

title: Self-Expanding Stent-Assisted Reconstruction of Distal Supra-Aortic Vessels in Acute Type A Aortic Dissection: A Comparative Analysis
authors: Bowen Li; Feng Shi; Zhipeng Hu; Zongli Ren; zhiyong wu; Luocheng Li; Zhiwei Wang
abstract: Background: Supra-aortic vessel reconstruction during total aortic arch replacement in acute Stanford type A aortic dissection patients with dissected distal supra-aortic vessels remains technically challenging; proximal supra-aortic vessel replacement alone carries a high risk of neurological complications secondary to intimal inversion. This study aims to evaluate clinical outcomes of self-expanding stent-assisted supra-aortic vessel reconstruction compared with proximal replacement of supra-aortic vessels alone. Methods and Results: We performed a single-center retrospective comparative analysis of 49 consecutive patients undergoing emergency total aortic arch replacement for acute Stanford type A aortic dissection from January 2022 to December 2023. Patients were divided into two groups according to intraoperative anatomy and surgeon decision: self-expanding stent-assisted supra-aortic vessel reconstruction (SAVR, n = 26) and proximal replacement of supra-aortic vessels alone (PRVA, n = 23). Neurological outcomes related to supra-aortic vessel intimal inversion, operative parameters, blood product transfusion, and short-term complications were analyzed. The mean follow-up was 18.2 ± 4.1 months (range, 12–24 months). The SAVR group exhibited significantly lower supra-aortic vessel stenosis rate (3.8% vs. 30.4%, p < 0.001) and zero cases of intimal inversion-related luminal collapse versus five cases in the PRVA group (0 vs. 5, p = 0.02). Numerically fewer cases of symptomatic stroke (0% vs. 8.7%, p = 0.09) and radiographic cerebral infarction (3.8% vs. 13.0%, p = 0.17) were observed in the SAVR group, though the differences did not achieve statistical significance. Red blood cell and fresh frozen plasma transfusion requirements, mechanical ventilation duration, and ICU stay length were significantly lower in the SAVR cohort. Cardiopulmonary bypass time and 30-day mortality were comparable between groups. Conclusions: Self-expanding stent-assisted supra-aortic vessel reconstruction represents a promising technical option during total arch replacement for acute Stanford type A aortic dissection with distal supra-aortic dissection, associated with superior branch vessel patency and favorable numerical trends in neurological and recovery-related endpoints, with a comparable early-term safety profile. Potential benefits require further validation in larger cohorts.

title: Early gains, late convergence: clinical and echocardiographic outcomes of TAVR versus SAVR in low-surgical-risk aortic stenosis: a meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis
authors: Ahmed Ebeid; Omar Ahmed; Amr Elghandour; Fares Alqammash; Mohamed Dawood; Abdelrahman A. Ebaid; Ahmed Shalaby; Ahmed Yasser; Heba Hrizat; Karam R. Motawea; Ibrahim Ebeid; Khaled Abouelmagd
abstract: TAVR is established in low-surgical-risk aortic stenosis, but the durability of its clinical benefits and hemodynamic profile across valve platforms remain uncertain. PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane Library were searched for randomized trials comparing TAVR with surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) in low-risk patients. Random-effects meta-analysis assessed clinical outcomes at 30 days, 1 year, and extended follow-up and echocardiographic outcomes at 30 days and 1 year, stratified by prosthesis type. Reconstructed individual patient data were analyzed for time-to-event endpoints, with trial sequential and sensitivity analyses. Seven RCTs ( n = 5,750; 2,927 TAVR, 2,823 SAVR) were included. At 1 year, TAVR reduced all-cause mortality (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.84; p = 0.0096), but not at extended follow-up (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.39; p = 0.65). Reconstructed IPD showed no significant hazard differences for mortality (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.21; p = 0.70), stroke (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.28; p = 0.85), or death/disabling stroke (HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.19; p = 0.91). RMST showed small 1-year advantages for mortality (0.1 months; p = 0.003) and death/disabling stroke (0.2 months; p < 0.001), neither sustained at extended follow-up. Major bleeding was lower with TAVR at 30 days, 1 year, and extended follow-up (RR 0.30, 0.32, and 0.32, respectively; all p ≤ 0.0004) and was the only outcome with conclusive trial sequential evidence. New-onset AF was lower with TAVR at 30 days (RR 0.19, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.36; p = 0.0012), 1 year (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.42; p = 0.0018), and extended follow-up (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.66; p = 0.0093), whereas pacemaker implantation was higher with TAVR at 30 days (RR 2.40, 95% CI 1.79–3.22; p = 0.0052), 1 year (RR 2.38, 95% CI 1.30–4.35; p = 0.0126), and extended follow-up (RR 2.04, 95% CI 1.57–2.64; p = 0.0005). Stroke, myocardial infarction, and valve reintervention did not differ significantly. Self-expanding valves had lower gradients with TAVR (− 2.10 mmHg), whereas balloon-expandable valves had higher gradients (+ 2.08 mmHg at 30 days; subgroup p < 0.0001). TAVR provides a modest, transient mortality benefit with less bleeding but greater pacemaker use; long-term outcomes remain comparable, and major bleeding was the only outcome with conclusive trial sequential evidence.

title: EFFECTIVENESS OF TOTAL ARTERIAL REVASCULARIZATION COMPARED TO SAPHENOUS VEIN GRAFT IN MULTIVESSEL CORONARY ARTERY BYPASS SURGERY : A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS AND PRIMARY STUDIES
authors: I GNA Bayu Wiradinatha; I Made Indra Prasetya
journal: The Indonesian Journal of General Medicine
abstract: Introduction: Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) remains the preferred revascularisation strategy for complex multivessel coronary artery disease, yet the great saphenous vein graft (SVG) is still used in the vast majority of operations despite its progressive late attrition. Total arterial revascularization (TAR), the complete avoidance of SVG, has been proposed to eliminate vein-graft failure, but its superiority rests largely on observational data. This review synthesised contemporary (2021-2026) randomised and primary evidence comparing TAR, or arterial-for-venous conduit substitution, with SVG-containing CABG.1–3 Methods: The study strictly adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs), prospective and retrospective cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies comparing TAR (or an arterial conduit replacing SVG) with SVG-containing CABG in multivessel disease were eligible. Results: Twenty-one reports (3 RCTs; 18 observational reports from 15 cohorts; 18 unique cohorts; approximately 73,700 patients from 14 countries) were included. In non-randomised cohorts, TAR was associated with lower long-term all-cause mortality (5 independent estimates; HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.76-0.99; p = 0.041; I² = 35.4%), but the association lost significance after HKSJ adjustment (95% CI 0.71-1.06) and the prediction interval crossed unity (0.61-1.24). Randomised comparisons of arterial versus venous conduits to the second target showed no mortality difference (HR 0.93, 0.62-1.40; I² = 75.2%), although RAPCO-SV demonstrated fewer 15-year major adverse cardiac events (HR 0.71, 0.52-0.98). Across all seven estimates the pooled HR was 0.89 (0.78-1.03). Within the Australian and New Zealand registry, the benefit was consistent in men (HR 0.86) and women (0.82), in patients aged 70 years or older (0.87) and younger (0.80), but not demonstrable when LVEF was below 30% (0.87, 0.67-1.13). Early outcomes favoured TAR in small cohorts (in-hospital death/MACCE RR 0.35, 0.15-0.80), with shorter ventilation, intensive care and hospital stay. No small-study effect was detected (Egger p = 0.91). Certainty of evidence was low to very low.8–13 Discussion: The survival signal favouring TAR is modest, driven predominantly by one large binational registry, susceptible to residual confounding and surgeon-selection bias, and is not confirmed by randomised conduit trials; conversely, no signal of harm emerged, and arterial strategies appeared safe with favourable perioperative profiles in experienced centres. Benefit appears most plausible in patients with long life expectancy and high-grade non-LAD target stenoses.2,14,15 Conclusion: Contemporary evidence supports TAR as a safe strategy associated with a modest long-term survival advantage in observational data, but high-certainty proof of superiority over SVG-containing CABG is lacking. Individualised conduit selection by an experienced heart team is recommended pending adequately powered RCTs such as the Total Arterial (TA) Trial.1,3

title: Exploring the application value of preoperative femoral artery and vein cannulation in redo cardiac surgery
authors: Yi Hui Yu; Xun Li Zhang; Lei Wang; Li Qiong Xiao; Fu Hua Huang; Zhen Hong Wang
abstract: BACKGROUND: To explore the clinical value of preoperative femoral vessel cannulation in redo cardiac surgery. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was performed on the clinical data of 106 patients who underwent redo cardiac surgery in our hospital from January 2022 to December 2024. According to the cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) cannulation technique adopted, the patients were divided into the Femoral Cannulation group (n = 79) and the Traditional Central Cannulation group (n = 37). Preoperative baseline data, intraoperative CPB-related parameters, blood product consumption, and the incidence of postoperative complications were recorded and compared between the two groups. RESULTS: There were no statistically significant differences in preoperative baseline data or intraoperative parameters between the two groups (all P > 0.05). Similarly, no significant statistical differences were found in postoperative mortality, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) utilization rate, acute kidney injury (AKI) incidence, or cognitive dysfunction incidence between the two groups. However, compared with the Traditional Central Cannulation group, the Femoral Cannulation group had significantly lower intraoperative packed red blood cell (PRBC) transfusion volume and a significantly lower incidence of major cardiovascular injuries (all P < 0.05). CONCLUSION: In redo cardiac surgery, preoperative femoral vessel cannulation can significantly reduce the incidence of major cardiovascular injuries and the demand for intraoperative blood transfusion, which is worthy of promotion and application in clinical practice.

title: Guide-sheath-assisted bailout technique for intra-procedural single-leaflet device attachment using the PASCAL system: a case report
authors: M Nukariya; Yuki Nishimura; Yoko Nakaoka; Kazuya Kawai; Hiroki Sugane
abstract: Abstract Background Single-leaflet device attachment（SLDA）is a rare but serious complication of mitral valve transcatheter edge-to-edge repair（MTEER）. When SLDA occurs after full device release, management options are limited. In contrast, intra-procedural SLDA recognized before full implant release may allow a specific bailout strategy. Case summary A 77-year-old man with severe degenerative mitral regurgitation (MR) underwent MTEER using the PASCAL Ace system because of high surgical risk. Initial device implantation reduced MR from severe to mild. However, after removal of both clasp lines during the release process, SLDA occurred at the posterior leaflet, resulting in recurrent severe MR. Although standard retrieval was no longer feasible, the implant remained connected to the steerable catheter. Under fluoroscopic and transesophageal echocardiographic guidance, a guide sheath was advanced coaxially toward the implant. Controlled insertion of the guide sheath between the clasp and paddle, followed by gradual paddle opening, enabled leaflet disengagement and successful device retrieval without leaflet injury. A second implantation achieved a sufficient reduction in mitral regurgitation. Discussion This case demonstrates a novel bailout technique for intra-procedural SLDA. Successful retrieval requires precise coaxial device alignment, careful catheter manipulation, continuous monitoring of leaflet tension, and meticulous guidance using fluoroscopy and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). Importantly, prompt recognition of SLDA by TEE is a prerequisite of this technique. In conclusion, the guide-sheath-assisted retrieval technique can represent a potential bailout strategy for intra-procedural SLDA before full implant release during MTEER.

title: Collagen and myocyte interplay in cardiac volume overload: a multi-constituent growth and remodeling framework
authors: L. Maga; Mathias Peirlinck; L. Noël
abstract: Abstract Hearts subjected to volume overload (VO) are prone to detrimental anatomical and functional changes in response to elevated mechanical loading, ultimately leading to heart failure. Experimental findings now emphasize that organ-scale changes following VO cannot be explained by myocyte growth alone, as traditionally proposed in the literature. Collagen degradation, in particular, has been associated with VO and assumed to play a central role in both its acute and chronic stages. This hypothesis, however, remains to be substantiated by comprehensive mechanistic evidence, and each constituent contribution to myocardial growth and remodeling (G&R) processes is yet to be quantified. In this work, we present a multi-constituent G&R framework that integrates a mixture-based constitutive model within the kinematic growth formulation. This framework enables us to mechanistically assess the relative contributions of collagen and myocyte changes to alterations in tissue properties, ventricular dimensions, and growth phenotype. Our numerical results confirm that collagen remodeling affects the passive mechanical response of the myocardium, whereas myocytes predominantly influence the extent and phenotype of VO-induced growth. Importantly, collagen degradation exacerbates myocyte hypertrophy, revealing a synergistic interplay that accelerates the left ventricular eccentric growth and thereby promotes systolic dysfunction. This work constitutes an important step towards an integrated characterization of the early compensatory stages of VO-induced cardiac G&R.

title: Mitral regurgitation and left atrial phasic function and atrioventricular coupling in patients with myocardial infarction: a cardiac magnetic resonance imaging study
authors: Xiaoling Wen; Guo Ying-kun; Yue Gao; Zhi-Gang Yang
journal: Quantitative Imaging in Medicine and Surgery
abstract: Background: Mitral regurgitation (MR) after myocardial infarction (MI) may increase left atrial (LA) pressure and contribute to cardiac dysfunction. This study evaluated the incremental association of MR with LA phasic function and strain and identified independent factors associated with LA deformation in patients with MI. Methods: This retrospective study included 189 patients with MI (111 without MR and 78 with MR: mild, 27; moderate, 33; severe, 18) and 86 normal controls who underwent 3.0-T cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). MR severity was graded by the CMR-derived MR fraction: mild <30%, moderate 30% to <50%, and severe ≥50%. CMR-derived LA phasic function and strain (reservoir strain, epsilon-s; booster strain, epsilon-a; conduit strain, epsilon-e), left ventricular (LV) function and strain, infarct size, and MR fraction were measured. Between-group comparisons were performed using one-way analysis of variance or the Kruskal-Wallis test with post hoc correction, and multivariable linear regression was used to identify independent factors associated with LA strain. A two-sided P<0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: Patients with MI and MR had lower LA reservoir strains [22.14%±10.91% vs. 28.65% (22.78%, 38.30%) vs. 41.70% (36.15%, 53.15%)], booster strains [11.52%±6.19% vs. 13.80% (10.20%, 19.80%) vs. 19.25% (15.10%, 24.05%)], and conduit strains [9.40% (6.03%, 14.85%) vs. 14.60% (9.60%, 20.50%) vs. 22.55% (17.75%, 30.43%)] than patients with MI without MR and controls (all P<0.05). They also had higher LA maximum volume [68.43 (57.44, 91.51) mL] and minimum volume [35.93 (24.43, 61.15) mL] and lower LA total ejection fraction (45.39%±14.97%) than the other groups (all P<0.05). In multivariable analysis, MR degree was independently associated with reservoir strain (β=−0.194, P=0.048) and conduit strain (β=−0.208, P=0.038). Anterior wall MI (reservoir strain: β=−0.245, P=0.014; booster strain: β=−0.231, P=0.028; conduit strain: β=−0.224, P=0.027) and posteromedial papillary muscle infarction (reservoir strain: β=−0.329, P=0.004; booster strain: β=−0.370, P=0.003) were also independently associated with LA strain. Conclusions: MR was associated with further deterioration of LA myocardial strain in patients with MI. Posteromedial papillary muscle infarction, anterior wall MI, beta-blocker use, and dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus clopidogrel were independently associated with LA strain. CMR-derived functional and strain parameters may help characterize LV-LA coupling and support risk stratification in this population.

title: Acute Changes in Left Atrial Appendage Flow Velocity During Pulsed Field Ablation: An Intraprocedural Intracardiac Echocardiography Study
authors: Yu Pan; Pavel P. Osmancik; Tomas Knize; Josef Hornof; Dalibor Heřman; Sabri Hassouna; Erika Slusnakova; Stepan Soukup; Marek Hozman
abstract: **Background:** Despite the close anatomical relationship between the left pulmonary veins (PVs) and the left atrial appendage (LAA), acute changes in LAA flow during pulsed field ablation (PFA) remain poorly characterized. **Objectives:** To characterize acute intraprocedural changes in LAA flow and transmitral filling during PFA for atrial fibrillation (AF) using paired intracardiac echocardiography (ICE). **Methods:** Patients with paroxysmal or persistent AF undergoing PFA were prospectively enrolled if they were in sinus rhythm at the beginning of the procedure. ICE was performed immediately before and after PFA to assess LAA emptying velocity (LAAEv), LAA filling velocity (LAAFv), transmitral E- and A-wave velocities, and E-wave deceleration time (EDT). Paired pre-to-post PFA changes were assessed, followed by a sensitivity analysis using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) and exploratory subgroup analyses. **Results:** Among 98 patients, LAAEv increased from 35.45 to 40.00 cm/s immediately after PFA (estimated paired increase, 4.95 cm/s; 95% CI, 2.35-7.80; P less than 0.001), while LAAFv increased by 4.36 cm/s (95% CI, 1.81-6.91; P=0.001). E-wave velocity increased by 8.69 cm/s and EDT decreased by 31.73 ms (both P less than 0.001), whereas A-wave velocity did not change significantly (P=0.08). In the ANCOVA model, changes in heart rate, systolic blood pressure, and vasopressor use were not significantly associated with changes in LAAEv. A marked acute reduction in LAAEv (20% or greater) occurred in 12 patients (12.2%). No significant subgroup interactions were observed. **Conclusions:** LAA flow velocities increased acutely after PFA, accompanied by changes in transmitral filling, although a minority of patients showed a marked acute reduction in LAA emptying.

title: Advantages and Limitations of the Use of Robots in Minimally Invasive Mitral Valve Repair: Results From a Matched Direct Comparison
authors: Kosuke Nakamae; Yoshitsugu Nakamura; Daiki Yoshiyama; Yuto Yasumoto; Miho Kuroda; Shintaro Sawa; Yuka Higuma; Kusumi Niitsuma; Masaki Ushijima; Akihiro Higashino; Yujiro Hayashi; Taisuke Nakayama; Hiroaki Yusa; Ryo Tsuruta; Yujiro Ito
journal: Innovations Technology and Techniques in Cardiothoracic and Vascular Surgery
abstract: Objective: To compare the surgical outcomes of nonrobotic and robotic minimally invasive mitral valve repair. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent minimally invasive mitral valve repair from January 2014 to March 2024. After excluding the learning curve cases, early and midterm outcomes were compared. Results: A total of 422 patients who underwent minimally invasive mitral valve repair (nonrobotic, n = 103; robotic, n = 319) were enrolled. The robotic group had a higher EuroSCORE II ( P < 0.001). After propensity matching, the final cohort included 84 and 168 patients in each group. In the robotic group after matching, concomitant procedures remained significantly more frequent ( P = 0.030). However, operative time ( P = 0.782) and cross-clamping time ( P = 0.452) were comparable, whereas cardiopulmonary bypass time was significantly longer in the robotic group ( P = 0.031). Postoperative blood transfusion ( P < 0.001), chest tube output within 24 h ( P < 0.001), and intensive care unit stay ( P = 0.042) remained higher in the robotic group after matching. Postoperative mitral regurgitation was no greater than mild in both groups ( P = 0.146). At 4 years, overall survival was 94.4% versus 98.4% ( P = 0.215), and freedom from recurrence of moderate or greater mitral regurgitation was 98.5% versus 97.9% ( P = 0.230) after matching. These results are consistent with those observed before matching. Conclusions: Robotic mitral valve repair demonstrated comparable perioperative and midterm outcomes despite greater transfusion requirements and a higher frequency of concomitant procedures. The higher rate of concomitant procedures should be interpreted with caution because it may partly reflect differences in surgical era and patient selection.

title: Exercise Echocardiography in the Diagnostic Work-up of Unexplained Dyspnoea: A Critical Narrative Review of Physiological Targets, Diagnostic Performance and Unresolved Controversies
authors: Malki Mohamed; Loudiyi Nadia; Lakhal Zouhair; Benyass Aatif
journal: Asian Journal of Research in Medical and Pharmaceutical Sciences
abstract: Background: Chronic exertional dyspnoea frequently remains unexplained after clinical assessment, natriuretic peptide measurement and resting echocardiography. Many underlying cardiovascular abnormalities, particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and exercise pulmonary hypertension, become apparent only during physiological stress. Exercise echocardiography is non-invasive, widely available and free of ionising radiation, but its diagnostic role outside ischaemia testing remains contested. Purpose and Scope: This critical narrative review evaluates the evidence supporting exercise echocardiography in adults with chronic exertional dyspnoea that remains unexplained after first-line evaluation. It examines test conduct and feasibility, the diastolic stress test, pulmonary vascular and right ventricular responses, ischaemic, valvular and dynamic obstructive causes, and multiparametric approaches incorporating lung ultrasound, cardiopulmonary exercise testing and artificial intelligence. Methods: Literature was identified through structured searches of bibliographic databases and scholarly indexes, supplemented by citation tracking and professional-society guidance. Evidence was appraised with attention to patient spectrum, reference standards, feasibility reporting and outcome relevance, and synthesised thematically. Principal Findings: Invasive studies consistently show that exercise unmasks haemodynamic abnormalities that resting tests miss. Exercise-derived echocardiographic abnormalities, including elevated filling-pressure surrogates, exercise pulmonary hypertension and exercise-induced pulmonary congestion, carry consistent prognostic information. The diagnostic accuracy of individual markers, especially the ratio of early mitral inflow to early diastolic annular velocity, is considerably less secure: validation studies conflict, largely because of differences in patient spectrum, reference standards and measurement timing. Tricuspid regurgitation signals are frequently unobtainable at peak exercise, and the incremental value of stress testing over probability scores appears modest in several invasive validation cohorts. Left atrial mechanics, systolic reserve, cardiac output-indexed pulmonary pressures and lung ultrasound show promise but require external validation. Unresolved Questions: Consensus is lacking on the reference standard, age- and sex-specific normal responses, optimal protocols and the effect of test-guided management on patient outcomes. Implications and Conclusion: Exercise echocardiography is best regarded as a question-driven, multiparametric physiological test integrated with pre-test probability and, where available, gas-exchange measurement, rather than as a single-parameter rule-in or rule-out tool. Prospective multicentre studies with invasive reference standards and outcome-oriented diagnostic trials are needed before stronger recommendations can be justified.

abstract: Antecedentes: La miocardiopatía hipertrófica (MCH) es la miocardiopatía hereditaria más frecuente y presenta importantes desafíos diagnósticos y terapéuticos en América Latina debido a la heterogeneidad en la disponibilidad de recursos, el acceso a tecnologías avanzadas y la organización de los sistemas de salud.Objetivo: Desarrollar el primer Consenso Interamericano sobre MCH con el propósito de protocolizar la atención de estos pacientes adaptado a la realidad regional.Métodos: La Sociedad Interamericana de Cardiología (SIAC) convocó un comité de expertos de distintos países de América.Se realizó una revisión sistemática de la evidencia, seguida de la elaboración de recomendaciones que fueron validadas mediante metodología Delphi, considerándose consenso un acuerdo superior al 80% de los participantes.Resultados: El consenso aborda de manera integral la evaluación y el manejo de la MCH, incluyendo epidemiología, fisiopatología, herramientas diagnósticas multimodales, genética y asesoramiento familiar, fenocopias, tratamiento farmacológico e invasivo, complicaciones asociadas, evaluación del riesgo de muerte súbita, poblaciones especiales (pediátricos y gestantes), ejercicio físico y estrategias de seguimiento.Asimismo, incorpora recomendaciones específicas orientadas a optimizar la implementación de estas estrategias en América Latina.Conclusiones: El Consenso Interamericano de MCH proporciona recomendaciones para el diagnóstico y tratamiento de esta patología, integrando la mejor evidencia disponible con la experiencia clínica regional y considerando las particularidades epidemiológicas, económicas y sanitarias de la región.Constituye un marco de referencia para homogeneizar la atención de pacientes con MCH y sus familias en América Latina.

title: Impact of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Burden on Echocardiographic Remodeling and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Hypertension
authors: Hyue Mee Kim; Minjung Bak; Jiesuck Park; Hong-Mi Choi; Yeonyee Elizabeth Yoon; Goo‐Yeong Cho; In‐Chang Hwang
abstract: Aims: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome highlights the interrelationship between metabolic, renal, and cardiovascular disorders. However, whether CKM burden influences longitudinal cardiac structural and functional recovery and subsequent cardiovascular outcomes remains unclear. Methods: We studied 1,600 patients from the STRATS-HHD registry who underwent echocardiography at baseline and 6-18 months after treatment initiation. CKM burden was defined by obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and severe hypertension (0-1, 2, or ≥3 components). The primary outcome was cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization (HHF). Results: CKM burden was 0-1 in 973 patients (60.8%), 2 in 440 (27.5%), and ≥3 in 187 (11.7%). Higher burden was associated with worse baseline cardiac abnormalities and increased primary outcome risk (adjusted HR, 3.09; 95% CI, 1.92-4.98 for ≥3 vs 0-1; adjusted HR, 1.53; 95% CI, 1.27-1.84 per +1 CKM component). The prognostic association persisted after additional adjustment for hepatic steatosis index-defined metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. Despite overall improvement in most echocardiographic parameters after treatment, patients with CKM burden ≥3 showed less favorable E/e′, LV global longitudinal strain (GLS), and LA stiffness index at follow-up. Normalization of these parameters at follow-up was associated with substantially lower subsequent cardiovascular risk. Mediation analyses suggested that echocardiographic abnormalities partially mediated the association between high CKM burden and the primary outcome. Conclusion: CKM burden identifies hypertensive patients with less favorable cardiac function after treatment and increased cardiovascular risk. These findings highlight the association of CKM burden with cardiac functional recovery and prognosis in patients with hypertension.

title: PASCAL Precision System Outcomes by Implant Location and Lesion Location in Degenerative Mitral Regurgitation Patients From the STS/ACC TVT Registry
authors: P. Kasi Ramanathan; Raj Makkar; Thomas E. Waggoner; Azeem Latib; Robert Kipperman; Ivan Hanson; Anjan Sinha; Tarun Chakravarty; Rahul P. Sharma; Jeremiah Peter Depta; Jorge Castellanos; Susheel Kodali; Amar Krishnaswamy; Brian K. Whisenant; Daniel S. Menees; David Scott Lim; Fahad Syed Gilani; Carlos E. Sanchez; Neil M. Renard; Gus Theodos; Ricardo Yaryura; Blake Gardner; Daniel Howard Steinberg; Eric Gnall; Georges Kaddissi; Adnan K. Chhatriwalla; Antonio Halais Frangieh; Mackram F. Eleid; Philippe Généreux; John Thomas Saxon; Pedro Arturo Villablanca; Fadi Matar; Himanshu Agarwal; Stan J. Chetcuti; Tiberio Frisoli; Firas E. Zahr
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
abstract: Background Mitral valve transcatheter edge‐to‐edge repair can be more challenging in noncentral regions of the valve and in anterior or bileaflet lesions. We assess effect of implant location and leaflet lesion location on safety and effectiveness of PASCAL Precision system in degenerative mitral regurgitation (MR). Methods Mitral valve transcatheter edge‐to‐edge repair outcomes in patients with degenerative MR treated with PASCAL Precision system (September 2022–October 2024), from the US STS/ACC TVT (Society of Thoracic Surgeons/American College of Cardiology Transcatheter Valve Therapy) Registry, were analyzed by implant location (A2P2/non‐A2P2) and leaflet lesion location (anterior/posterior/bileaflet). Procedural, clinical, and echocardiographic outcomes to 30 days were assessed. Results At 30 days, both A2P2 (n=1526) and non‐A2P2 (n=299) groups had low event rates (cardiovascular mortality: 1.1% versus 1.0%, mitral valve reintervention: 0.4% versus 0.0% and single leaflet device attachment: 0.5% versus 0.3%; all P >0.05) and demonstrated significant MR reduction ( P <0.001 versus baseline) with no significant difference between groups ( P =0.750) (MR ≤2+: 93.4% versus 95.4%; MR ≤1+: 72.0% versus 73.3%). Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary scores improved significantly in both groups (∆19.3, ∆17.7 points; P =0.741). The anterior (n=250), posterior (n=902), and bileaflet (n=192) disease groups also had low event rates (cardiovascular mortality: 0.4%, 1.1%, 0.0%; mitral valve reintervention: 0.8%, 0.1%, 0.5%; and single leaflet device attachment: 0.8%, 0.2%, 0.5%; all P >0.05), and demonstrated significant MR reduction ( P <0.001 versus baseline) with no significant difference across groups ( P =0.459) (MR ≤2+: 94.1%, 93.1%, and 94.5%; MR ≤1+: 79.0%, 69.2%, and 72.4%). All groups experienced significant improvement in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary scores (∆21.4, ∆18.8, ∆12.0 points; P =0.087). Conclusion In real‐world patients with degenerative mitral regurgitation, treatment with the PASCAL Precision system was associated with favorable safety and effectiveness at 30 days, regardless of implant location or leaflet lesion location.

title: The predictive value of the hemodynamic profile for survival in patients undergoing transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair
authors: Felix Ausbuettel; Fares Kano; Nikolaos Patsalis; Christin Fichera; Dimitar Divchev; Carlo-Federico Fichera
abstract: Transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair (M-TEER) represents a safe treatment modality for patients with high-grade mitral regurgitation (MR). While clinical decision-making concerning the referral of suitable candidates for M-TEER is guided primarily by clinical and echocardiographic parameters, the potential of hemodynamic parameters obtained at the time of screening in predicting treatment outcomes has not been sufficiently investigated. All patients who underwent M-TEER and who provided sufficient right heart catheterisation (RHC) data prior to M-TEER were enrolled for analysis. The investigated hemodynamic parameters were analysed descriptively and their associations with survival were estimated by univariable Cox regression analysis and Kaplan–Meier’s analysis. A total of 94 patients were analysed, of whom 92.6% (87/94) had concomitant pulmonary hypertension (PH). Analysis of the hemodynamic profile revealed that 46.8% (44/94) of patients had advanced-stage congestive heart failure with a cardiac index < 2 L/min/m2, and 68% (64/94) of patients had a cardiac power index <0.5 W/m2. According to the results of the Kaplan–Meier and Cox regression analyses, a systolic pulmonary artery pressure (sPAP) > 60 mmHg and a mean right atrial pressure (RAP) > 20 mmHg were proven to be significant predictors of long-term survival after M-TEER. Analysis of the hemodynamic profile, specifically the identified predictors, contributes to the improved identification of scenarios associated with a favourable prognosis in patients undergoing M-TEER. CI: cardiac index; CPI: cardiac power index; meanRAP: mean right atrial pressure; M-TEER: transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair; PH: pulmonary hypertension; RHC: right heart catheterisation; sPAP: systolic pulmonary artery pressure.

title: Beyond flow: a ventricular-load framework for VA-ECMO in cardiogenic shock
authors: Rachid Attou; Sébastien Redant; Ikram Boutrika; Sohaïb Mansour; Mohamed El Mallouli; Leticia Al Kai; Ayoub Jaafari
abstract: Cardiogenic shock still carries a 30-day mortality of approximately 40%–50% despite reperfusion, vasoactive support and modern intensive care. Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) can rapidly restore systemic perfusion, but recent randomised evidence has reframed its role. In infarct-related shock, randomised trials have not shown a clear survival benefit from routine early VA-ECMO; ECLS-SHOCK and pooled analyses also found more bleeding and vascular complications. In the same period, DanGer Shock showed that a primary microaxial-pump (Impella CP) strategy improved survival in a carefully selected population with ST-elevation myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock, although it was tested against standard care rather than head-to-head against VA-ECMO and does not isolate unloading as the causal mechanism. Read together, these data motivate the central argument of this review: peripheral VA-ECMO is usefully managed not only as a problem of circulatory flow, but also as a dynamic problem of ventricular loading. We advance this as an organising framework rather than as a demonstrated mechanism, since differences in patient selection between these trials offer a competing and equally tenable explanation. Retrograde aortic return increases effective LV afterload, while venous drainage reduces preload; the clinical result depends on the interaction between circuit flow, native contractility and biventricular loading conditions. This narrative, non-systematic review synthesises contemporary trial evidence, the physiology and treatment of LV loading, and approaches to serial assessment of the supported heart, from haemodynamics and bedside echocardiography to emerging deformation and advanced imaging tools. VA-ECMO should therefore be viewed as a time-limited bridge whose net benefit depends on reversible disease, early recognition of clinically relevant ventricular overload and repeated assessment of recovery, escalation options and futility.

title: Evaluation of echocardiographic abnormalities and associated factors in 100 hemodialysis patients
authors: Hakimeh Saadatifar; Khojasteh Marashi; Zahra Eslamifar; Saber Rostami; Aziz Kasani; Soraya Khajehrezaei
abstract: Abstract Background Systematic assessment of cardiac remodeling in hemodialysis (HD) patients is essential for cardiovascular risk stratification. Echocardiography is a widely available tool for evaluating structural and functional cardiac abnormalities. We investigated associations between clinical and dialysis-related parameters and echocardiographic abnormalities among patients receiving chronic HD at the Dezful Nephrology Center in southwestern Iran. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 160 adults undergoing chronic HD were screened and 100 met the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. All participants underwent transthoracic echocardiography. Associations between echocardiographic abnormalities and age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, body mass index (BMI), dyslipidemia, coronary and non-coronary vascular disease, dialysis access type, dialysis vintage, anemia, plasma lipid concentrations, and resting heart rate were evaluated Bivariate analyses were followed by multivariable logistic regression for prespecified binary echocardiographic outcomes. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. A two-sided P -value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Echocardiographic abnormalities were present in 86% of patients. After multivariable adjustment, hypertension (aOR 2.80, 95% CI 1.30–6.00), coronary artery disease (aOR 6.10, 95% CI 1.90–19.60), non-coronary vascular disease (aOR 4.20, 95% CI 1.30–13.60), and lower plasma triglycerides (aOR 0.99 per mg/dL, 95% CI 0.98–0.995) were independently associated with left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Diabetes was associated with diastolic dysfunction (aOR 2.60, 95% CI 1.10–6.20) and moderate-to-severe mitral or tricuspid regurgitation (aOR 2.40, 95% CI 1.00–5.70). Dialysis access type and non-coronary vascular disease were linked to left ventricular hypertrophy. Lower plasma triglycerides, higher resting heart rate, and non-coronary vascular disease were associated with right ventricular abnormality. Lower BMI and lower plasma triglycerides were associated with a higher aortic index. Traditional risk factors together with dialysis-related parameters, particularly low serum triglycerides, low BMI, and arteriovenous fistula access, showed independent associations with specific echocardiographic phenotypes. Conclusion Echocardiographic abnormalities are highly prevalent in this HD cohort and independently associated with both traditional cardiovascular risk factors and selected dialysis-related parameters, including low plasma triglycerides, low BMI, and the presence of arteriovenous fistula. These findings support closer clinical attention to these variables for cardiac risk stratification in hemodialysis patients. Given the cross-sectional design and modest sample size, the results represent associations rather than causal effects. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Association between autoimmune diseases and risk of developing breast cancer-related lymphedema
authors: Benjamin D. Wagner; Stav Brown; Andrea Veronica Barrio; Thomas Amburn; Natália Polidorio; Tiana Le; Lilian Boe; Raghu P. Kataru; Geoffrey E. Hespe; Michelle R Coriddi; Danielle H. Rochlin; Hidehiko Yoshimatsu; Babak Joseph Mehrara
abstract: Abstract Preexisting autoimmune disease may increase susceptibility to breast cancer-related lymphedema (BCRL) through chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation, but its association with BCRL risk is poorly understood. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults undergoing sentinel lymph node biopsy and/or axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer at a tertiary cancer center between 2010 and 2021. Autoimmune diseases were identified using International Classification of Diseases (ICD)-9/10 codes, and the primary outcome was BCRL diagnosis based on ICD codes. Associations between autoimmune disease and time to BCRL were evaluated using univariate and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models. Among 20,027 patients with a median follow-up of 61.7 months (IQR, 38.7–94.2), 1361 (6.8%) had a preexisting autoimmune disease and 1728 (8.6%) developed BCRL at a median of 17.4 months (IQR, 8.0–33.9) after surgery. In multivariable analysis, autoimmune disease was independently associated with increased BCRL risk (hazard ratio [HR], 1.52; 95% CI, 1.30–1.77; P < .001). Elevated risks were observed for rheumatoid arthritis (HR, 1.54), autoimmune thyroiditis (HR, 1.40), Graves’ disease (HR, 1.49), multiple sclerosis (HR, 1.87), systemic lupus erythematosus (HR, 2.46), and systemic sclerosis (HR, 2.10). These findings suggest autoimmune disease may be an independent risk factor for BCRL and may improve risk stratification.

title: Digoxin Revisited: An Updated Review in the Light of Recent Trials
authors: Muhammad Saad; Muhammad Abdullah; Ankit Yelamarthy; Krystal John; Abbas Hayat Mallick; Behram Khan; Hassan Tahir; Rajan Krishnamani
abstract: Isolated from Digitalis species following William Withering’s 1785 work on foxglove, digoxin inhibits myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase, raising intracellular calcium and vagal tone to produce inotropic, rate-controlling, and neurohormonal-deactivating effects. The foundational DIG trial (1997) showed no mortality benefit but reduced heart failure hospitalizations, prompting a progressive guideline downgrade. Three decades later, DIGIT-HF (2025, digitoxin) and DECISION (2026, low dose digoxin) retested cardiac glycosides atop modern four pillar guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT). DIGIT-HF significantly reduced the composite of death or worsening heart failure (hazard ratio (HR), 0.82), while DECISION showed a numerical but nonsignificant benefit. A pooled meta-analysis of DIG, DIGIT-HF, and DECISION (9,013 patients) confirmed a consistent 15% reduction in worsening heart failure events across three decades of changing background therapy, without a significant mortality effect. The Dig-RHD trial addressed an unstudied population: symptomatic rheumatic heart disease (RHD), a chronic valvular heart disease that results from permanent damage to cardiac valves due to group A streptococcal infection. RHD affects roughly 40 million people and causes approximately 300,000 deaths annually, disproportionately in low- and middle-income countries. In 1,769 patients randomized across 12 Indian centers, digoxin significantly reduced the composite of death or new-onset/worsening heart failure (31.4% vs. 35.5%; HR, 0.82; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.70 to 0.97; P = 0.02), with greater benefit in atrial fibrillation, women, and patients with low body mass index (BMI), and a number needed to treat of approximately 14 over 2 years. Digoxin is not a mortality-reducing drug, but pooled contemporary evidence establishes it as a reproducible, low-cost tool for reducing heart failure events, now supported for the first time by high-quality randomized data in RHD, a population with substantial global burden and no prior evidence-based medical therapy. These findings warrant reconsideration of digoxin’s guideline status and development of RHD-specific recommendations.

title: Troponin I and CPK-MB in Chronic Kidney Disease Stage IV and V
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
abstract: Background: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated with a markedly increased risk of cardiovascular disease, particularly coronary artery disease (CAD).Interpretation of cardiac biomarkers in CKD is challenging because reduced renal clearance may result in elevated baseline levels.This study evaluated the utility of Troponin I (Trop I) and Creatine Kinase-MB (CK-MB) in detecting CAD among patients with CKD Stage IV and V. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted in the Departments of General Medicine, Cardiology, and Nephrology at Vydehi Institute of Medical Sciences and Research Centre from March 2023 to August 2024.Ninety patients aged >18 years with CKD Stage IV or V were enrolled.Demographic details, clinical history, laboratory investigations, serum creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), Troponin I, CK-MB, electrocardiography, and two-dimensional echocardiography findings were recorded.Comparisons were made between patients with and without CAD.Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to assess the diagnostic performance of Troponin I. Results:The mean age of participants was 58.93 ± 12.00 years, and 71.1% were males.CAD was present in 28 (31.1%)patients.Serum creatinine and eGFR were comparable between CAD and non-CAD groups (p>0.05).Mean Troponin I levels were significantly higher in patients with CAD than those without CAD (1.10 ± 1.18 vs. 0.04 ± 0.05 ng/mL; p<0.001).In contrast, CK-MB levels did not differ significantly between groups (4.71 ± 6.47 vs. 3.73 ± 3.44 ng/mL; p=0.352).ROC analysis demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance of Troponin I for predicting CAD, with an AUC of 0.946, sensitivity of 89.29%, specificity of 98.39%, and an optimal cut-off value of >0.15 ng/mL.Conclusion: Troponin I is a reliable and clinically useful biomarker for detecting CAD in patients with CKD Stage IV and V, whereas CK-MB has limited diagnostic value.Troponin I may aid cardiovascular risk stratification when interpreted alongside clinical and imaging findings.

title: Interpretable computational SHG microscopy enables quantitative tissue phenotyping of cardiac remodeling in nonischemic heart failure
authors: Reid Master; Wesley Poon; Rania Uzma; Stephan Bannikov; Muthu Kumar Krishnamoorthi; Ashok Veeraraghavan; HONG ZHAO; Arvind Bhimaraj; Raksha Raghunathan; Stephen TC Wong
abstract: Heart failure is characterized by extracellular matrix remodeling and collagen deposition that impair myocardial function. Second harmonic generation (SHG) microscopy provides label-free visualization of fibrillar collagen and myosin but lacks standardized, interpretable, and quantitative frameworks with clinical-level performance. We present a feature extraction pipeline integrating 87 biologically interpretable SHG-derived metrics for automated classification of nonischemic heart failure in murine specimen. The framework distinguished normal, heart failure, and natural recovery states with area-under-the-curve values of 0.84-0.99, outperforming established open-source SHG feature extraction tools. These findings support interpretable, SHG-based quantification of cardiac remodeling and establish a methodology for future multimodal biophotonics applications.

title: Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance in MINOCA and Acute Myocarditis: A Comparative Multiparametric Evaluation
authors: Chiara Tognola; Francesca Daus; Stefano Pedroli; Davide Paolo Bernasconi; Paola Sormani; Ilaria Bassi; Angela Milazzo; Giuseppina Quattrocchi; Cristina Giannattasio; Patrizia Pedrotti
journal: The International Journal of Cardiovascular Imaging
abstract: Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) and acute myocarditis (AM) often present with overlapping clinical features and biomarker profiles, making early differential diagnosis challenging. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) is the reference modality for etiological assessment through functional evaluation and multiparametric tissue characterization. The aim of this study was to compare clinical and CMR characteristics of patients with MINOCA and suspected AM, and to identify imaging features enabling accurate differentiation. We retrospectively analyzed 127 consecutive patients undergoing CMR (February 2021-October 2024): 62 with suspected MINOCA and 65 with suspected AM. Clinical data, laboratory findings, ECG, and CMR parameters (cine imaging, T1/T2 mapping, extracellular volume [ECV], and late gadolinium enhancement [LGE]) were assessed. MINOCA patients were older (median 59 years) and predominantly female (64.5%), whereas AM patients were younger (median 29 years) and mainly male (81.5%). AM was associated with higher troponin and inflammatory markers. Among patients initially referred with suspected MINOCA, LGE was present in 50.0%, compared with 93.8% of those referred with suspected acute myocarditis (p < 0.001). MINOCA showed predominantly ischemic LGE patterns, while AM exhibited non-ischemic subepicardial or mid-wall LGE with myocardial edema. CMR confirmed myocardial infarction in 48.4% of patients and identified alternative diagnoses in 41.9%, while 9.7% had normal CMR findings. Multiparametric CMR reliably distinguishes ischemic from inflammatory myocardial injury in patients with chest pain, elevated troponin, and non-obstructive coronaries. Early CMR integration improves diagnostic accuracy and supports tailored management.
